title: God's works and kingdom praised through all generations
english: All these things are alike in their human elements, but they are indications of divine activity that is fearful, strong, and destructive of humans (Ps 143:4-5).

In the present life these words could apply to one human being after another in succession, because as the earlier ones depart, there are others who take their place in their territory. For this reason we are all called by the name of Adam, as being those very ones, and God says, "I made the earth and humanity upon it," reckoning all as one (Ps 144:1). But in the life to come these things are true for each individual as well, as he praises God continually and eternally, and because it is not sufficient to praise for a short time, the worshiper adds, "Forever and to the age of the age" (Ps 144:4).

Since everything God made remains forever, according to Ecclesiastes, each generation that sees his works praises them, seeing that they receive praise beyond all praise. And they declare your power, by which you brought them into existence. This is the wisdom by which you made all things, and your power and wisdom is your only-begotten Son; for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

They make known that he holds dominion over all things, even if he does not yet reveal this, since humans are not yet able to receive it (Ps 144:9, 12). For humans are too small for the greatness of the divine kingdom to be shown in them; therefore he adds what is fitting for God (Ps 144:12).
When he speaks of the opening of God's hands as the provision of food for created things, he clearly is not presenting bodily hands but likening the creative power in this way (Ps 144:16; Ps 144:17).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

Re-read 2026-10-09 (Densify): the earlier English had major meaning errors in almost every section; replaced by the work_pipeline translation from the locked Greek (Pass A gloss, Pass B English, per-section two-family check), then re-gated clause by clause; see reviews/fix-notes-2026-10-09-reread.md.
orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 143-144, explaining how the psalm's words about God's works, kingdom, and provision apply both to this present life and to the future eternal life.
